title: In 1920 He Helped Bury Romania's Leading Marxist. In 1937 He Was Painting the King's Own Palace.
standfirst: This undated landscape falls inside the two years Ion Theodorescu-Sion spent travelling Romania with the painter Camil Ressu — the same two years he helped organise a trade union and, by one account, helped bury a Marxist theorist. Within two decades he was decorating the king's own palace, and died months after his magazine's editor cheered the king's new single-party state.

sections.heading: An Undated Canvas, Placed by Where He Was Standing
sections.body: No one wrote a year on this small oil-on-cardboard landscape, and Sion didn't put one on it himself. The one detailed account of it, [a 2011 auction catalogue](https://harmonious-dream-ha5-efahrfwj.on-forge.com/en/auction/licitatia-de-impresionism-si-postimpresionism-romanesc-36-2011-1/lot/ion-theodorescu-sion-case-la-amiaza-efect-de-soare-en-35595), places it instead by context: the years right after the First World War, when Sion resumed painting in earnest and travelled Romania gathering landscapes, roughly two of those years spent working alongside the painter Camil Ressu around Brașov and the southern Carpathians. Call it 1919 to 1921. That is also, as it happens, the exact window in which the man later remembered as the painter of a reactionary literary magazine was doing close to the opposite of that — helping organise a trade union and, by one account, arranging a Marxist theorist's funeral.

sections.heading: The Scholarship He Was Sent to Paris to Waste
sections.body: Long before any of that, the state had paid for his education and watched him more or less throw it back. From 1904 to 1907 a Ministry of War scholarship sent him to Paris to study under Jean-Paul Laurens and Luc-Olivier Merson at the École des Beaux-Arts — training meant to produce a dependable academic painter for a dependable state institution. Instead, according to [his biographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_Theodorescu-Sion), he turned rebellious, picked up socialist sympathies, and wasted the scholarship outright; his patrons dropped him, and he went on to French Algeria afterward, possibly to enlist in the Foreign Legion — the record doesn't settle whether he actually did. Nothing about the decade that followed suggests he had been tamed. When Romania entered the First World War in 1916, he was drafted, and the army's Chief of Staff, Dumitru Iliescu, put him to work depicting Romanian forces in action rather than firing on them himself. It didn't spare him the collapse: he watched the front give way and retreated with the army into Moldavia, ending up in Iași, the temporary capital of what was left of the Romanian state. It was there, in 1918, that he co-founded the Arta Română group together with [Camil Ressu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camil_Ressu), the painters Ștefan Dimitrescu and Nicolae Tonitza, and the sculptor Oscar Han — a professional association, not a party, but one built by painters who had all just watched the same catastrophe from the same retreating road.

sections.heading: In 1920 He Helped Bury a Man Born Solomon Katz
sections.body: Two years after Iași, by the account of the writer Tudor Teodorescu-Braniște, Sion was among those who helped arrange the funeral of [Constantin Dobrogeanu-Gherea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantin_Dobrogeanu-Gherea), who had died in Bucharest on 7 May 1920. Gherea — born Solomon Katz — was the single most influential Marxist theorist Romania had produced: his circle had built the Romanian Social-Democratic Workers' Party and argued down both the anarchists and the agrarian Narodniks who competed with it for the same audience. A year later Sion co-founded, with Ressu and the painter Arthur Verona, what is recorded as Romania's first artists' trade union. None of this reads like the opening chapters of a man who would spend his final years as a favoured painter of a king's single-party state. It is, in fact, exactly that man's opening chapters.

sections.heading: A Magazine Found Him Before Its Editor Did
sections.body: Gândirea did not start out as the magazine history remembers it. Founded in Cluj in 1921 as a modernist, expressionist-leaning literary supplement, it only began turning toward mystical Romanian nationalism after the critic Nichifor Crainic joined its leadership in 1926 and became its director and ideological guide two years later, according to [the magazine's own history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A2ndirea). Sion had already been welcomed into its pages before any of that happened: in 1925 its art columnist, Oscar Walter Cisek, reviewed his show at the Ileana Gallery warmly, and the state itself bought one of the paintings on view there, a still life called Roz și roș, on the recommendation of the official Ion Lapedatu. By the time Crainic had full control of the magazine, Sion was already established as exactly the kind of painter it wanted representing it: what his own biographers now describe as the visual component of the neo-traditionalist, Romanianist, neo-Byzantine current Gândirea had organised around itself.

sections.heading: The Party He Lived to See Was the King's, Not Yet the Guard's
sections.body: By the early 1930s, the magazine Crainic ran had stopped being simply traditionalist. He welcomed Hitler's rise to power in 1933, and by 1938 was praising Mussolini in print: "Mussolini does not terrorize," he wrote that year, "for Mussolini does not kill." Gândirea had already been shut once, in 1933–34, after Crainic was implicated in the trial over the assassination of a Romanian prime minister by Iron Guard gunmen. Sion's own standing, meanwhile, moved from the magazine's pages into the state's actual buildings: in 1937 he was among the artists chosen to paint four decorative panels for the Throne Hall of the Royal Palace in Bucharest, the king's own residence, and that same year he was registered by government ordinance as a state-approved church muralist. The single-party state the Gândirea circle ended up endorsing that decade was not, yet, the Iron Guard's own. On [16 December 1938](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Renaissance_Front), days after having the Guard's leadership killed in custody, King Carol II founded the National Renaissance Front as Romania's only legal party, built explicitly to starve the Guard of the ground it had been gaining. Sion, according to his own biographers, spent his last years sympathising with precisely that — Carol's royal, anti-Legionary authoritarianism, not the movement it had been built to replace. He died in Bucharest on 31 March 1939, three and a half months after the Front's founding. Crainic's own obituary for him, printed in Gândirea that May, opened without ceremony: "Theodorescu-Sion died unexpectedly, in the full summer of his life."

sections.heading: A Debate That Started After He Could Answer It
sections.body: He did not live to see how much further his own magazine would travel. In 1941, two years after his death, Crainic marked Gândirea's twentieth anniversary with a line that left no ambiguity: "Judaism was our most bitter enemy," he wrote. "Not an adversary, but an enemy." The magazine had by then lined up behind Ion Antonescu's antisemitic government. Sion's own reputation fell almost as fast as the regime that outlived him did. Later critics, by his own biographers' account, have kept arguing over what to make of a painter who moved, within two decades, from a wasted socialist scholarship and a Marxist theorist's funeral to the house style of a nationalist magazine — and over how far to tie him personally to the far right its editor increasingly embraced. No source consulted here settles that question, and the honest position is that it remains open. What isn't in doubt is this undated little landscape's own moment: painted somewhere in the two years when none of it had happened yet, while he was still burying Marxists and founding unions instead of decorating palaces.
